newsitem.title: CHINA: HK June trade figures expected to disappoint.
newsitem.headline: HK June trade figures expected to disappoint.

text.p: Hong Kong external trade statistics due out on Tuesday are expected to disappoint, led by the crucial re-export sector, economists said on Monday.

Lingering economic weakness in Europe and a temporary slowdown in Japan in the second quarter suggests initial expectations for trade performance in June were too optimistic, said Clive McDonnell, economist at Crosby Securities.
"Hong Kong is not performing so much badly as maybe our expectations were running a little bit high in terms of the re-export growth we were expecting for the year," he said.

Re-exports are goods shipped to China for processing and then re-exported through Hong Kong. They account for the vast majority of the territory's trade, with a value of HK$1,186 billion in 1995 out of total exports of HK$1,398 billion.
June re-exports are expected to continue the declining growth trend shown in April and May, economists said.
"The trade sector is not as good as I would like," said Guanon Ma, economist at Bankers Trust in Hong Kong.
In addition to slack demand from Hong Kong's major re-export destinations, Ma said re-export growth is declining as China becomes more competitive.
"My feeling would be that China increasingly is improving the efficiency of its ports and trade machine and therefore will become less dependent upon Hong Kong as a major trade entrepot," Ma said.

Countering the negative trade performance, May retail sales figures released on Friday indicated rising consumer confidence in Hong Kong, although economists differed on whether the trend was sustainable through to the end of the year.
Hong Kong's May retail sales totalled a provisional HK$19.7 billion, up 10 percent in value on the year and up six percent on the month.
Celebrations marking Hong Kong's return to Chinese sovereignty on July 1 were partly responsible for the strong May showing, said another economist who declined to be named.

"This return of consumer confidence is fuelled by low inflation, low unemployment and a resumption of the feelgood factor on the absence of worries about handover and China, as well as robust stock and property markets," he said.
The consumption-led recovery that has marked Hong Kong's economic performance so far this year can be expected to continue, he said.
Ma agreed that the trend is positive, but disagreed on its cause.
"I do not put a political interpretation on it," he said. "I wouldn't say it's a sign of confidence over the post-'97 future. I would say it is a natural sign of an economy on a cyclical upswing."

McDonnell, who agrees with the government's GDP estimate for 1997, does not believe the trend can continue. He believes many Hong Kong residents "front-loaded" their purchases through the first half of the year.
"I think it will be difficult for volume sales to grow as robustly as they did during May," he said.
